h1:
Sakon Nakhon–Kalasin
On the Sahatsakhan Dinosaur Trail
intro: If you've already done Sakon Nakhon and want to stretch the trip a little longer, point the car south toward Kalasin. It's about 128 km from downtown Sakon Nakhon, roughly a 2-hour drive, and what's waiting is something Kalasin has that other places don't: a real dinosaur burial site, excavated right where the bones were found and kept on display in the ground at Phu Kum Khao in Sahatsakhan district, home of the Sirindhorn Museum. This is a 3-day, 2-night cross-province plan: spend the first day on Sakon Nakhon's best bits, then cross over to Sahatsakhan at your own pace, with opening hours, entry fees, routes and eateries we've actually checked.

blocks.html: This trip suits anyone starting from Sakon Nakhon who wants an unusual end point and has their own car or a rental — the Sahatsakhan sights are spread out around Lam Pao Dam and no public transport reaches every stop. The main route leaves Sakon Nakhon city on Highway 213 heading south, passes through Somdet district into Kalasin town, then turns off to Sahatsakhan, the dinosaur country. We've set it up so you cover Sakon Nakhon city on day one, cross provinces on the morning of day two, then loop back on day three.

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: The Sirindhorn Museum (Phu Kum Khao) is closed every Monday, except when Monday is a public holiday. If you don't want to miss the trip's highlight, don't schedule your Sahatsakhan day on a Monday. It's open Tuesday–Sunday, 9:00 AM–5:00 PM. Renting a car in Sakon Nakhon runs about 800–1,200 THB a day, and you should fill the tank before leaving the bigger towns.

blocks.text: Day 1 — The best of Sakon Nakhon town

blocks.html: No need to cross provinces on day one. Spend the time making the most of Sakon Nakhon's highlights first. Phra That Choeng Chum and Nong Han Lake are the two stops you shouldn't skip here, then cap the day with a Phon Yang Kham beef dinner — the province's signature dish.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Sakon Nakhon town — Phra That Choeng Chum · Nong Han · Phon Yang Kham beef

items.activity: Start at Wat Phra That Choeng Chum Worawihan in central Sakon Nakhon, paying respects at the Phra That Choeng Chum stupa and Luang Pho Phra Ong Saen, the city's revered Buddha images.
items.note: It's an ancient sacred site, believed to hold the footprints of four Buddhas beneath the stupa. Free entry, open roughly 6:00 AM–6:00 PM. Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered.

items.activity: Stroll Somdet Phra Srinagarindra Park (Sra Phang Thong) on the edge of Nong Han Lake and catch the breeze off the water in the middle of town.
items.note: This lakeside park has a red-lotus pond and a fountain mid-water. Free entry, an easy walk on from the stupa. Photograph the view over Isan's largest freshwater lake before you head off.

items.activity: Stop for lunch and try local Phu Tai cooking — things like mok no mai (bamboo shoots steamed with bai yanang leaf), wai curry, or freshly cooked khao hang rice.
items.note: Sakon Nakhon food is bold in the proper Isan way, and local-style spots are easy to find around town. Figure on a couple hundred baht per head per meal.

items.activity: Drop by an indigo-dye shop in town to pick up genuine Sakon Nakhon kram (indigo-dyed) cloth as a souvenir.
items.note: There are several indigo shops in a row downtown. Indigo scarves start around 250 THB, dyed shirts from around 500 THB. Real indigo has a soft scent and a muted blue, not the harsh tone of chemical dye.

items.activity: Dinner of Phon Yang Kham fattened beef, Sakon Nakhon's signature, eaten jim jum (herbal hotpot) or grilled at the Phon Yang Kham cooperative restaurant in town.
items.note: Phon Yang Kham beef is well-bred fattened cattle raised in Ban Phon Yang Kham — tender, nicely marbled, and far more affordable than imported beef.

blocks.title: Where to sleep the first night
blocks.html: Stay in Sakon Nakhon town the first night for convenience — there are hotels across a range of budgets, all close to restaurants — and save your energy for the cross-province drive next morning. If you'd rather save time, you can drive down to Kalasin in the evening and sleep near Sahatsakhan instead.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Cross to Kalasin for dinosaurs at Phu Kum Khao

blocks.html: Today is the heart of the trip. Leave Sakon Nakhon a little early, drive about 128 km south into Kalasin town, then turn off to Sahatsakhan district — the place that earned Kalasin its name as Isan's dinosaur city. Real driving time is about 2.5 to 3 hours including rest stops.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Sakon Nakhon → Sahatsakhan — Sirindhorn Museum · Wat Phutthanimit Phu Khao (~150 km)

items.activity: Leave Sakon Nakhon on Highway 213 heading south through Somdet district toward Kalasin, then continue on into Sahatsakhan district.
items.note: Grab breakfast before you go and fill the tank. It's a main highway the whole way, an easy drive, with gas stations at intervals.

items.activity: Reach the Sirindhorn Museum (Phu Kum Khao), the trip's highlight — three buildings and eight zones telling the story from the birth of the planet to the dinosaurs, with both models and real skeletons.
items.note: Open Tuesday–Sunday, 9:00 AM–5:00 PM, closed Monday. Entry for Thais is 40 THB for adults, 10 THB for children; for foreigners, 100 THB for adults, 50 THB for children. The highlight is the skeleton of Phuwiangosaurus sirindhornae, a plant-eating dinosaur named after HRH Princess Sirindhorn.

items.activity: Walk over to the real dinosaur dig site on Phu Kum Khao, where researchers uncovered bones lying in the rock layer.
items.note: Bones were first found here around 1994 and excavation has since turned up more than 700 pieces, making it one of Thailand's most complete plant-eating dinosaur sites. You see the real remains in the exact position they were dug up, not just replicas.

items.activity: Lunch around Sahatsakhan — try fish from Lam Pao Dam, like blanched Lam Pao barramundi with dipping sauce, or tom yum fish.
items.note: Lam Pao Dam is a major freshwater fish-breeding ground, so the restaurants here get fresh fish, cooked bold in the Isan style.

items.activity: Stop at Wat Phutthanimit (Phu Khao), about 7 km from the district town, to see an ancient reclining Buddha carved into the rock face — lying on its left side, gilded all over.
items.note: This reclining Buddha is unusual in lying on its left side, a rare pose, and without the usual pillow. Legend says it was carved in the same era as Phra That Phanom. Open daily, roughly 6:00 AM–6:00 PM, in a shady, peaceful setting up on Phu Khao.

items.activity: Check into your lodging on the Kalasin/Sahatsakhan side, then head out in the evening to watch the sunset over Lam Pao Dam.
items.note: You can sleep around Sahatsakhan or head back into Kalasin town — they're about 30 km apart. Kalasin town has more hotels and restaurants to choose from, while Sahatsakhan is closer to the next day's sights.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Tep Suda Bridge, Lam Pao Dam, then loop back

blocks.html: On the last day, take in the Lam Pao Dam views and Tep Suda Bridge, Sahatsakhan's landmark, drop by the dinosaur park for photos, then pick up souvenirs and drive back to Sakon Nakhon or carry on. No need to rush — the sights all sit close together around the dam.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Sahatsakhan — Tep Suda Bridge · Dinosaur Park · Souvenirs, then loop back

items.activity: Head to Tep Suda Bridge, the roughly 2,040-metre bridge across Lam Pao Dam, where both railings are cast in dinosaur shapes as a symbol of Kalasin.
items.note: It's the longest bridge over freshwater in Thailand, with a wide view of the dam stretching to the horizon. Early morning is cool and breezy, the sun still soft — good for photos.

items.activity: Stop at the Sahatsakhan Dinosaur Park to photograph the big dinosaur statues of various species, then settle into a café on the edge of Lam Pao Dam.
items.note: The Sahatsakhan side has several lake-view cafés — some are floating bamboo cafés that look out at Tep Suda Bridge. Sip a coffee with the view at easy prices; weekdays aren't crowded.

items.activity: Lunch by Lam Pao Dam — order grilled prawns, grilled fish and som tam, eaten over the water view.
items.note: The lakeside garden restaurants have over-the-water seating, a cool, easy atmosphere, with fish and prawns fresh from the dam.

items.activity: Buy souvenirs before you go — Phu Tai prae wa silk, smoked fish sausage, and Isan jaew bong chilli paste.
items.note: Prae wa is Kalasin's renowned handwoven silk, while smoked catfish sausage keeps longer than fresh goods and travels easily.

items.activity: Set off home — loop back to Sakon Nakhon in about 2.5–3 hours, or continue to Khon Kaen / Udon Thani to catch a flight back.
items.note: For flying home, the nearest and most convenient airports are Sakon Nakhon, Udon Thani and Khon Kaen. Pick the one that fits your booked flight.

blocks.title: How real are the dinosaurs here
blocks.html: Phu Kum Khao is one of Thailand's most complete real dinosaur dig sites, where multiple Phuwiangosaurus sirindhornae specimens were found lying together in the same rock layer. The museum is built right over the excavation pit. Kids who love dinosaurs get a real kick out of it, because they see the actual remains, not just models.

blocks.text: Food across both provinces you shouldn't miss

blocks.html: A cross-province trip has the edge of letting you eat both Sakon Nakhon and Kalasin specialties on one run. The Sakon Nakhon side stands out for Phon Yang Kham beef and Phu Tai dishes; the Kalasin side for freshwater fish from Lam Pao Dam and smoked souvenirs. Here's the list we've ranked by how worth a try each one is.

items.name: Phon Yang Kham fattened beef (Sakon Nakhon)
items.blurb: Well-bred fattened cattle from Ban Phon Yang Kham, tender with lovely marbling, eaten jim jum (herbal hotpot) or grilled at the Phon Yang Kham cooperative restaurant in Sakon Nakhon town. The signature dish you have to try here.

items.name: Blanched Lam Pao barramundi (Kalasin)
items.blurb: Fresh freshwater fish from Lam Pao Dam, blanched just until done so the flesh stays sweet and tender, eaten with a punchy seafood dipping sauce. It's the dish several lakeside restaurants recommend in agreement.

items.name: Grilled prawns by Lam Pao Dam (Kalasin)
items.blurb: Big prawns grilled over flame and eaten with a tangy dip, at lakeside garden restaurants like Klin Lamduan on the way to Lam Pao Dam in Yang Talat district, with over-the-water seating and wide views.

items.name: Mok no mai bai yanang (Sakon Nakhon)
items.blurb: A local Phu Tai dish of Sakon Nakhon — bamboo shoots boiled with bai yanang leaf and Phu Phan herbs, mellow and distinctly fragrant, eaten with hot sticky rice.
items.meta: Local food · restaurants across Sakon Nakhon town

items.name: Tam Yua Ye, Kalasin town
items.blurb: A som tam shop in Kalasin town on Pradit Road. Standouts are boiling seafood som tam, crispy noodle som tam with cockles, and noodle som tam with fresh prawns — punchy and bold, just right for som tam fans.
items.meta: Som tam shop · Pradit Road, Kalasin town

items.name: Khao hang (Sakon Nakhon)
items.blurb: A Phu Tai folk-wisdom rice — paddy is steamed before milling, giving fragrant rice high in nutrients. Cook it as your everyday rice or buy a bag to take home as a souvenir.

items.name: Jaew hon, Kalasin Isan hotpot
items.blurb: A pot of jim jum with bold herbal broth — dip beef and vegetables into the hot pot. It's the supper Kalasin locals gather over in the cool of the evening, by the dam or in town.

items.name: Smoked fish sausage (Kalasin souvenir)
items.blurb: Sausage made from smoked catfish until fragrant, a renowned Kalasin souvenir. Easy to take home and keeps longer than fresh goods.

items.name: Lam Pao pickled fish (seasonal souvenir)
items.blurb: Pla som made from freshwater fish of Lam Pao Dam, naturally fermented for a sour tang. Sold at souvenir shops in some seasons. Fry or steam and eat with hot rice.
items.meta: Seasonal souvenir · around Lam Pao Dam

blocks.text: What's there in Sahatsakhan besides dinosaurs

blocks.html: A lot of people come to Sahatsakhan for the dinosaurs alone, but the area around Lam Pao Dam actually has other sights close by that you can add on if you have time on day two or three.

items.name: Tep Suda Bridge
items.blurb: A roughly 2,040-metre bridge across Lam Pao Dam, the longest freshwater-crossing bridge in Thailand, with railings cast in dinosaur shapes — Sahatsakhan's main photo spot.

items.name: Lam Pao Dam
items.blurb: A large earthen dam that doubles as a freshwater fish-breeding ground. Around it you'll find Dok Ket Beach, cafés and waterside restaurants for a relaxed sit-down.

items.name: Wat Phutthanimit (Phu Khao)
items.blurb: A temple atop Phu Khao with an ancient reclining Buddha carved into the rock face, lying on its left side in a rare pose, gilded all over, in a quiet, shady setting.

items: Car/fuel — car rental around 800–1,200 THB a day, split between you; fuel for the Sakon Nakhon–Kalasin–Sahatsakhan round trip runs about 700–1,000 THB per car.
2 nights' lodging — hotels in Sakon Nakhon or Kalasin town start around 500–900 THB, stepping up to 1,000–1,800 THB a night for nicer ones.
Entry fees — the Sirindhorn Museum is 40 THB for Thai adults, 10 THB for children, while Phra That Choeng Chum, the Nong Han lakeside park, Wat Phu Khao and Tep Suda Bridge are all free.
Food for 3 days — Isan dishes, fattened beef and dam fish, around 700–1,100 THB.
Souvenirs — Sakon Nakhon indigo cloth, Kalasin prae wa silk, fish sausage, jaew bong — budget more as you like.

blocks.text: Why it's worth crossing over to Kalasin

blocks.html: To be straight about it, Kalasin isn't a place people deliberately fly in to visit on its own — but tacked on after Sakon Nakhon, just a 2-hour drive away, it's very much worth it, because what's here you can't get elsewhere. The dinosaur dig pit on Phu Kum Khao is the real thing, excavated on site, not just replicas. Kids who love dinosaurs get hugely excited, while adults pick up easy-to-grasp geology. Add Tep Suda Bridge and Lam Pao Dam, which give wide views of a different kind from Sakon Nakhon's Nong Han, and altogether it's a trip you can tell your friends took you to dinosaur country.

blocks.title: Best time to go
blocks.html: Late rainy to early cool season (November–February) is best — pleasant and cool, good for being outdoors at both Phu Kum Khao and the lakeside. Don't forget the Sirindhorn Museum is closed on Mondays; if your Sahatsakhan day lands on a Monday you'll miss out. In the hot season the sun on the hills is fierce, so do Phu Kum Khao and Wat Phu Khao in the morning, skip midday, and carry water and a hat.

If you only have 2 days, cut the Sakon Nakhon day, drive down to Kalasin first thing on day one, sleep one night in Sahatsakhan, and on the morning of day two visit the Sirindhorn Museum and dig site, drop by the dinosaur park for photos, then loop back over Tep Suda Bridge — enough to catch all the dinosaur highlights. But if you want both Sakon Nakhon and Kalasin without rushing, this 3-day, 2-night plan is just right: no more than two or three hours' driving a day, leaving plenty of time for actual sightseeing.

faq.q: How far is it from Sakon Nakhon to Kalasin, and how long is the drive?
faq.a: From downtown Sakon Nakhon to Kalasin town is about 128 km, roughly a 2-hour drive on an easy main highway, passing through Somdet district before reaching town. Sahatsakhan district, the dinosaur country, is about another 30 km out from Kalasin town, so Sakon Nakhon to Sahatsakhan is around 2.5–3 hours of real driving. Having your own car or a rental is the most flexible way to do it.

faq.q: When is the Sirindhorn Museum (Phu Kum Khao) open, and how much is entry?
faq.a: It's open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:00 AM–5:00 PM, closed Monday, except when Monday is a public holiday. Entry for Thais is 40 THB for adults, 10 THB for children; for foreigners, 100 THB for adults, 50 THB for children. Avoid scheduling your visit for a Monday, since you won't get in.

faq.q: Do you actually see real dinosaur remains at Phu Kum Khao?
faq.a: Yes, you do. The Sirindhorn Museum is built right over the excavation pit where multiple Phuwiangosaurus sirindhornae dinosaurs were found lying together in the rock layer, with more than 700 pieces dug up. Beyond the replicas and skeletons inside the buildings, you can walk over and see the real bones in the position they were unearthed — the thing that sets this place apart from an ordinary museum.

faq.q: How many days is ideal, and is it fun for kids?
faq.a: 3 days and 2 nights is just right: day one covers Sakon Nakhon town, day two crosses provinces for the dinosaurs and Wat Phutthanimit Phu Khao, and day three takes in Tep Suda Bridge and Lam Pao Dam before looping back. Kids who love dinosaurs have a great time, seeing the real skeletons, the dig site and the big statues in the dinosaur park. If time is tight you can squeeze it into 2 days and 1 night, but you'll have to rush and drive a lot in a single day.

faq.q: Do you need your own car, or can you use public transport?
faq.a: You really should have your own car or a rental, because the Sahatsakhan sights — the museum, Tep Suda Bridge and Lam Pao Dam — are spread around the dam and no public transport reaches every stop. Intercity buses run between Sakon Nakhon and Kalasin, but connecting on into Sahatsakhan is awkward. Without a car you may have to charter a local vehicle from Kalasin town in stages.
